scenes.title: Every standard halves the bits
scenes.narration: Every new video coding standard roughly halves the bits needed for the same picture quality. VVC, finalized in 2020, needs forty to fifty percent fewer bits than its predecessor HEVC. The price is computation: the VVC encoder is about ten times more complex, and the decoder about twice. This thesis is about paying that complexity in silicon.

scenes.title: How a codec works
scenes.narration: A codec works block by block. It predicts the block from what was already coded, keeps only the difference, and transforms that difference so its energy gathers in one corner. Quantization then turns most of the values into zeros, and only the few that remain are written as bits. The decoder reverses these steps, and the encoder contains a complete decoder of its own.

scenes.title: What VVC adds, and what the thesis builds
scenes.narration: VVC adds two transform tools, the Multiple Transform Selection and the Low-Frequency Non-Separable Transform, and a new in-loop filter, the Adaptive Loop Filter. They bring real compression gains, and they are expensive in hardware. This thesis designs exactly these three tools, for the decoder and for the encoder.

scenes.title: Why a chip
scenes.narration: Live video must be delivered on time, every frame. Software cannot reach a codec's best quality in real time, so professional encoders use dedicated hardware. An application-specific integrated circuit does the same work at a small fraction of the energy of a processor. The price is that nothing can be changed after manufacture.

scenes.title: The contract: samples per cycle
scenes.narration: The chip decodes 4K video at sixty frames per second with a clock of 450 megahertz. Expressed per clock cycle, the transform must absorb four samples every cycle, and every block size must take the same number of cycles, so that the modules chain without stalling. Within that contract, the score is chip area, memory and power.

scenes.title: The transform in silicon
scenes.narration: The transform is a matrix multiplication. Instead of hard-wiring every constant, the design uses sixty-four shared multipliers that read their coefficients from a small read-only memory. This takes sixty-three percent less silicon than the multiplier-less design. The second transform, LFNST, was added in the same way, the first hardware LFNST in the literature.

scenes.title: A filter that learns
scenes.narration: The Adaptive Loop Filter is a seven by seven diamond whose coefficients are chosen by the encoder and sent in the bitstream. Every four by four block is classified into one of twenty-five classes, and the kernel is rotated or flipped to match the block. One engine with twenty-six multipliers filters luma, chroma, and the cross-component filter.

scenes.title: The memory problem
scenes.narration: To filter one block, the filter needs the eight blocks around it, so blocks must wait in memory. Feeding the filter one Cr block, one Cb block, then two luma blocks keeps the co-located luma in the pipeline, and only two lines of blocks need to be stored. The memory drops by seventy-five percent.

scenes.title: The results
scenes.narration: All designs run at 450 megahertz on a 28 nanometre process, with a fixed latency, and were verified bit for bit against the reference software. They were integrated in a professional real-time encoder and decoder, and they led to four peer-reviewed publications and three firsts in the literature.

scenes.title: People and record
scenes.narration: The thesis was directed by Daniel Ménard and Olivier Déforges, and supervised by Wassim Hamidouche, at the IETR laboratory of INSA Rennes. It was defended in Rennes on the thirty-first of May 2022, and the full manuscript is open access.
